blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Everything below concerns equations in which each unknown appears on its own, multiplied by a number and added — the only kind this book uses.

An equation may hold two unknowns. On its own such an equation does not fix either of them.

A system of two equations in two unknowns is a pair of equations required to hold at the same time. A solution of the system is a pair of values that satisfies both equations, not one.

Two methods solve such a system. Substitution rearranges one equation to give one unknown in terms of the other, and puts that expression into the second equation, which then holds one unknown. Elimination adds a multiple of one equation to the other, choosing the multiple so that one unknown cancels.

A system of two such equations has exactly one solution, or none, or infinitely many. It has none when the two equations make statements that cannot both be true. It has infinitely many when one equation is a multiple of the other, and so states nothing the first did not.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The section before this one solved equations with one letter in them. This one starts where a line has two.

Here is such a line.

x + y = 10

Ask what x is. There is no single answer. Try some pairs and see.

x y
1 9
4 6
7 3

One equation with two unknowns does not pin either of them down. It ties them together. Fix one and the other follows; fix neither and you have nothing.

Now add a second statement that has to be true at the same time.

x + y = 10
x minus y = 4

Now there is one pair that works, and only one. Two statements, two unknowns.

There are two ways to find it, and they are the same idea approached from different sides.

The first is substitution. You have substituted a number for a letter before now. This is the same move with an expression in place of the number, and what it leaves behind is algebra rather than arithmetic.

Rearrange one equation so that one letter stands alone, then put that into the other equation.

Rearrange the first line to give x on its own.

x = 10 minus y

Now put that in place of x in the second line.

10 minus y minus y = 4
10 minus 2y = 4
2y = 6
y = 3

Then go back and get x.

x = 10 minus 3
x = 7

The second way is elimination. Add the two equations together, left to left and right to right. The y and the minus y cancel.

2x = 10 plus 4
10 plus 4 = 14
14 divided by 2 = 7

So x is 7. Elimination has found one unknown, and it is not finished. Put the 7 back into either line to get the other. The first line is the simpler one.

7 + y = 10
10 minus 7 = 3

So y is 3, the same as substitution gave. Now check. Put both numbers into both statements, not into one of them.

7 plus 3 = 10
7 minus 3 = 4

Both hold, so the pair is the solution.

Adding worked because one line had plus y and the other had minus y. When the same letter carries the same number and the same sign in both lines, subtract instead. Take one line from the other, left from left and right from right.

x + y = 10
x + 3y = 16

Take the first line from the second. The x terms cancel, and 3y take away y leaves 2y.

16 minus 10 = 6
2y = 6
6 divided by 2 = 3

So y is 3. Put it back into the first line to get x.

10 minus 3 = 7

So x is 7. Check the pair in both lines.

7 plus 3 = 10
3 times 3 = 9
7 plus 9 = 16

And sometimes no letter carries matching numbers at all. Then make a match. Multiply every term of one line, on both sides, by the same number. That is the rule from the section before this: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

x + y = 10
3x + 2y = 27

The second line has 2y and the first has only y. So multiply the whole of the first line by 2.

2 times 10 = 20
2x + 2y = 20

Now the y terms match. Take this new line from the second line. The 2y terms cancel, and 3x take away 2x leaves x.

27 minus 20 = 7

So x is 7. Put it back into the first line to get y.

10 minus 7 = 3

So y is 3. Check the pair in both lines.

7 plus 3 = 10
3 times 7 = 21
2 times 3 = 6
21 plus 6 = 27

The same pair sits behind all three examples, so you can watch each method land on it. Every elimination has the same four steps. Make one letter match, if it does not already. Add or subtract the lines so that it cancels. Solve for the letter that is left. Then put that value back into either line to get the other.

Sometimes no whole-number multiple of one line matches the other. Then multiply both lines, each by its own number.

2x + 3y = 12
3x + 2y = 13

Multiply the whole of the first line by 3 and the whole of the second by 2. Both x terms become 6x.

6x + 9y = 36
6x + 4y = 26

Take the second new line from the first. The 6x terms cancel, and 9y take away 4y leaves 5y.

36 minus 26 = 10
5y = 10
10 divided by 5 = 2

So y is 2. Put it back into the first line to get x.

3 times 2 = 6
12 minus 6 = 6
6 divided by 2 = 3

So x is 3. Check the pair in both lines.

2 times 3 = 6
3 times 2 = 6
6 plus 6 = 12
3 times 3 = 9
2 times 2 = 4
9 plus 4 = 13

Two more shapes to recognise, because they arrive without warning.

Sometimes the second statement repeats the first.

x + y = 10
2x + 2y = 20

The second line is the first line doubled. It is true whenever the first is true, so it adds nothing, and you are back to as many answers as you like.

And sometimes the two statements cannot both hold.

x + y = 10
x + y = 12

Two numbers cannot add to 10 and to 12. There is no pair at all, and the useful thing to say is not the answer but that one of the two statements is wrong.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
A packet reaches you with two lines of its panel gone. The energy is still there, 468 kilocalories in every 100 grams, and so is the protein, 12 grams. The carbohydrate line and the fat line have torn away. Those figures are made up for this problem. The label rule is the real one you have used in the two sections before this.

E = 4c + 4p + 9f

Put in what the panel still gives you.

4 times 12 = 48

Take that 48 off both sides.

468 minus 48 = 420

So what you know is this.

4c + 9f = 420

One line, two unknowns.

Look at three pairs that all satisfy that line.

carbohydrate grams fat grams from carbohydrate from fat total
60 20 240 180 420
105 0 420 0 420
15 40 60 360 420

Every row is a genuine answer to the arithmetic. Not every row is a possible packet. The second row puts 105 grams of carbohydrate and 12 grams of protein into 100 grams of food. The section before this taught you to throw out a negative mass, and this row fails the same kind of test. Run that second check on any answer, because the arithmetic never runs it for you.

So what would fix them? A second statement that has to be true at the same time.

Suppose the maker tells you the carbohydrate is three times the fat. Write it beside the first.

4c + 9f = 420
c = 3f

Now substitute. Put 3f in place of c in the first line, so 4c becomes 4 times 3f.

4 times 3f, plus 9f = 420
12f + 9f = 420
21f = 420

What went in for c here was a single term, 3f. Often it is a difference instead, such as 75 minus f. Then it goes in inside brackets, and you expand them as the section on variables showed. Every term inside is multiplied by the 4.

4(75 minus f) = 300 minus 4f

Back to the packet. Divide both sides by 21.

420 divided by 21 = 20

Twenty grams of fat. Now go back for the carbohydrate.

3 times 20 = 60

Sixty grams of carbohydrate.

Check both numbers in both statements. Checking one is not checking the pair.

4 times 60 = 240
9 times 20 = 180
240 plus 180 = 420

The first statement holds. And 60 is three times 20, so the second holds as well.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The second statement was handed to you here. In real work it has to come from somewhere, and where it came from is the part that decides whether your answer means anything.

points.html: One equation with two unknowns has many answers, not one. Anyone who reads a single relationship as fixing a single quantity is reading something that is not there.
Count the unknowns and count the equations before you start.
Check a solved pair in both equations.
When somebody draws a conclusion about one quantity from a single relationship, ask what the second statement is and where it came from.

Two statements pin two unknowns down only when they say different things. Two that repeat each other leave you with as many answers as before. Two that contradict each other leave you with none, which is itself worth reporting.

Use substitution when one equation already has a letter standing nearly alone. Use elimination when the same letter carries matching numbers in both lines. Use it too when you can make them match by multiplying one whole line by a number.
Solving a pair tells you what follows from the two statements, and nothing about whether either is true.

blocks.prompt:
A district officer shows you one line from a planning note.

Every meal served costs us the grain plus the cooking fuel, and the two together come to 18 rupees a meal.

They then ask you how much the grain alone costs.

Say what you can and cannot answer from that line. Then say exactly what one further piece of information would let you answer it, and give two different forms that piece could take.
blocks.answer:
What the line gives you is a relation between two quantities. Call the grain cost g and the fuel cost k, both in rupees a meal.

g + k = 18

What you can say: the grain cost and the fuel cost add to 18 rupees a meal. So neither of them can be more than 18, and if one goes up the other must come down by the same amount.

What you cannot say: what the grain costs. Any pair adding to 18 fits this line, and the line carries nothing that prefers one pair to another.

What would settle it is a second statement about the same two quantities, true at the same time. It could take either of these forms, among others.

The first form names one of them outright.

k = 5

Then the grain cost follows at once.

18 minus 5 = 13

The second form relates them again, differently.

g = 2k

Then substitute and solve.

2k + k = 18
3k = 18
18 divided by 3 = 6

The fuel is 6 rupees and the grain is 12.

18 minus 6 = 12

What matters in the answer you give the officer is the order of the two sentences. First: I cannot answer that from this line. Second: here is what I would need. Giving a number instead would be inventing one.

blocks.prompt:
A journalist has three minutes and no appetite for algebra. They have been told two things about a scheme. Its total spend went up, and its total number of meals went up. They want to write that the cost of each meal went up.

Explain why that does not follow, in words they can use, with one sentence they could quote.
blocks.answer:
Three minutes, no symbols, and one picture.

Start with the shape of what they have. Two numbers went up. The thing they want to write about is a third number, built out of both. Knowing that two numbers rose does not tell you what happened to something made by dividing one by the other.

Give them a case they can hold. Say a scheme spent more money and served more meals, and that the meals went up faster than the money. Then the cost of each meal went down while both totals went up. Nothing in the two rising figures rules that out.

Then say what would settle it. The spend in each year and the meal count in each year, all four numbers. With those, the cost of a meal in each year is one division, and the comparison is a fact rather than a guess.

The quotable sentence: “Two totals going up tells you nothing about the cost of a meal. The four numbers that would settle it take a morning to get.”

What not to say: do not say the claim is false. You do not know that either. You know it does not follow. That is a different statement, and a stronger one. It survives whatever the four numbers turn out to be.

blocks.prompt:
Two statements have to hold at the same time.

x + y = 7
x minus y = 1

Say for each of these pairs whether it is a solution.

x y
4 3
5 2
6 1
blocks.answer:
Test each pair in both statements.

The first pair.

4 plus 3 = 7
4 minus 3 = 1

Both hold, so this pair is a solution.

The second pair.

5 plus 2 = 7
5 minus 2 = 3

The first holds and the second does not, because 3 is not 1. So this pair is not a solution.

The third pair.

6 plus 1 = 7
6 minus 1 = 5

Again the first holds and the second does not. Not a solution.

Notice that all three pairs passed the first test. That is exactly why a pair is checked in both statements and never in one.

blocks.prompt:
Write down four different pairs of numbers that make this statement true.

x + y = 12

Then say how many such pairs there are, and what that means about what this one line can tell you.
blocks.answer:
Four pairs, and any four will do.

x y
0 12
3 9
5 7
10 2

Check one of them.

5 plus 7 = 12

How many are there: as many as you like. Pick any number for x at all and subtract it from 12 to get y, and the pair works. There is no end to them.

What that means: this line cannot tell you what x is. It can only tell you what y is once somebody else has told you x. One statement, two unknowns, no answer.

blocks.prompt:
Solve this pair by substitution.

y = 2x
x + y = 18
blocks.answer:
The first line already has y standing alone, so put 2x in place of y in the second line.

x + 2x = 18
3x = 18

Divide both sides by 3.

18 divided by 3 = 6

So x is 6. Now go back to the first line for y.

2 times 6 = 12

So y is 12.

Check the pair in both statements.

6 plus 12 = 18

And 12 is twice 6, so the first statement holds too.

blocks.prompt:
Solve this pair by elimination.

x + y = 15
x minus y = 3
blocks.answer:
Add the two statements together, left side to left side and right side to right side. The y on the first line and the minus y on the second cancel each other.

2x = 15 plus 3
15 plus 3 = 18
18 divided by 2 = 9

So x is 9. Put that into the first statement to get y.

15 minus 9 = 6

So y is 6.

Check the pair in both statements.

9 plus 6 = 15
9 minus 6 = 3

Both hold.

Why elimination was the easier route here: the y carried the same number in both lines. One line had a plus and the other a minus. So adding removed it in a single step. Had neither letter matched, you would have had to make a match first by multiplying a whole line.

blocks.prompt:
A panel gives the energy as 440 kilocalories in every 100 grams and the protein as 10 grams. The carbohydrate line and the fat line are missing. A note attached to the packet says the carbohydrate and the fat together weigh 75 grams. All four figures are made up for this problem.

Using the factors the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 set for calculating declared energy, work out the carbohydrate and the fat. Show every line and check the pair in both statements.
blocks.answer:
Write the label rule and take the protein term out of it.

E = 4c + 4p + 9f
4 times 10 = 40
440 minus 40 = 400

So the first statement is this.

4c + 9f = 400

The note gives the second statement.

c + f = 75

Rearrange the second to put c on its own, then substitute it into the first.

c = 75 minus f
4 times the whole of 75 minus f, plus 9f = 400

Work the bracket out. Four times 75 is 300, and four times minus f is minus 4f.

4 times 75 = 300
300 minus 4f + 9f = 400
300 + 5f = 400

Take 300 off both sides, then divide by 5.

400 minus 300 = 100
100 divided by 5 = 20

Twenty grams of fat. Now the carbohydrate.

75 minus 20 = 55

Fifty-five grams of carbohydrate.

Check the pair in both statements.

4 times 55 = 220
9 times 20 = 180
220 plus 180 = 400

55 plus 20 = 75

Both hold.

blocks.prompt:
Schedule II of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets two figures you need here. The hot cooked meal for lower primary classes is 450 kilocalories. The one for upper primary classes is 700 kilocalories.

A kitchen serves 50 meals in a day, some lower primary and some upper primary, and its plan totals 27,500 kilocalories for the day. The 50 and the 27,500 are made up for this problem.

Work out how many meals of each kind the plan is for. Show every line, and check the pair in both statements.
blocks.answer:
Name the two unknowns. Let L stand for the number of lower primary meals and U for the number of upper primary meals.

The first statement is the count of meals.

L + U = 50

The second is the total kilocalories, with each meal carrying its own figure from Schedule II.

450L + 700U = 27,500

Rearrange the first statement and substitute into the second.

L = 50 minus U
450 times the whole of 50 minus U, plus 700U = 27,500

Work the bracket out.

450 times 50 = 22,500
22,500 minus 450U + 700U = 27,500

The two U terms collect into one.

700 minus 450 = 250
22,500 + 250U = 27,500

Take 22,500 off both sides, then divide by 250.

27,500 minus 22,500 = 5,000
5,000 divided by 250 = 20

Twenty upper primary meals. Now the lower primary count.

50 minus 20 = 30

Thirty lower primary meals.

Check the pair in both statements.

30 plus 20 = 50

450 times 30 = 13,500
700 times 20 = 14,000
13,500 plus 14,000 = 27,500

Both hold. The two figures from Schedule II come from the Act. The split of 30 and 20 is your own arithmetic on a made-up plan. Say so whenever you quote it.

blocks.prompt:
Schedule II of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets four figures you need here. The hot cooked meal for lower primary classes is 450 kilocalories and 12 grams of protein. The one for upper primary classes is 700 kilocalories and 20 grams of protein.

A kitchen’s day sheet gives only two totals: 27,500 kilocalories and 760 grams of protein. The meal count has not been written down. Both totals are made up for this problem.

Work out how many meals of each kind the sheet describes. Use elimination rather than substitution. Show every line, and check the pair in both statements.
blocks.answer:
Let L stand for the number of lower primary meals and U for the number of upper primary meals. Each kind carries its own pair of figures from Schedule II, so each total gives you one statement.

450L + 700U = 27,500
12L + 20U = 760

To eliminate U, make the U terms match. The first line carries 700U and the second carries 20U, so multiply the whole of the second line by 35.

20 times 35 = 700
12 times 35 = 420
760 times 35 = 26,600

So the second statement, multiplied through, says this.

420L + 700U = 26,600

Now subtract that from the first statement, left from left and right from right. The U terms cancel.

450 minus 420 = 30
27,500 minus 26,600 = 900
30L = 900

Divide both sides by 30.

900 divided by 30 = 30

Thirty lower primary meals. Now go back for U, using the protein statement.

12 times 30 = 360
760 minus 360 = 400
400 divided by 20 = 20

Twenty upper primary meals.

Check the pair in both statements.

450 times 30 = 13,500
700 times 20 = 14,000
13,500 plus 14,000 = 27,500

12 times 30 = 360
20 times 20 = 400
360 plus 400 = 760

Both hold. Notice what you were given and what you were not: no meal count at all, and two totals of different kinds. Two totals were enough, because energy and protein are different statements about the same two unknowns.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

two statements have to hold at the same time
x + y = 20
x minus y = 6
rearrange the first statement
x = 20 minus y
put that into the first statement
20 minus y + y = 20
20 = 20
so both statements hold whatever y is
and any pair adding to 20 will do
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the sixth line. The rearranged first statement was put back into the first statement.

That can only ever give something true and useless. The rearranged line says the same thing as the line it came from, so putting one into the other says it twice. The 20 equals 20 that came out is not a finding. It is the working going round in a circle.

The whole point of substituting is to carry what you learned from one statement into the other one. Put the rearranged first line into the second.

20 minus y minus y = 6
20 minus 2y = 6

Take 20 off both sides, then divide by minus 2. Easier still, add 2y to both sides and take 6 off both sides.

20 minus 6 = 14
2y = 14
14 divided by 2 = 7

So y is 7. Now go back for x.

20 minus 7 = 13

So x is 13.

Check in both statements.

13 plus 7 = 20
13 minus 7 = 6

Why it looks reasonable: every line of the working is a true statement, and the last line is the truest of all. Nothing was miscalculated. A reader watching for arithmetic errors finds none. The error is in which statement the substitution went into, and the page does not label them.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a note carries two statements about a kitchen’s day
the lower primary and upper primary meals together number 50
L + U = 50
twice the lower primary meals and twice the upper primary meals together number 100
2L + 2U = 100
that is two statements and two unknowns, so the pair can be solved
from the first, L = 50 minus U
put it into the second
2 times the whole of 50 minus U, plus 2U = 100
100 minus 2U + 2U = 100
100 = 100
so L is 25 and U is 25
blocks.answer:
Two things broke, and the second one is the one that matters.

The first is the last line. The working reached a statement that is true for every pair, and then a pair was named anyway. Nothing in the working produced 25 and 25. The numbers were chosen because the two unknowns looked symmetrical.

The second is upstream, and it is why the working could not have ended any other way. The second statement is the first statement doubled. Multiply the first by 2 and you get the second exactly, so the second says nothing the first did not already say.

50 times 2 = 100

So this is one statement written twice, not two statements. Two unknowns and one statement means many answers, and 25 with 25 is only one of them.

30 plus 20 = 50
10 plus 40 = 50

Both of those pairs satisfy the note just as well as 25 and 25 does.

What a real second statement would look like: one that says something the first cannot. A total of kilocalories for the day does that, because a lower primary meal and an upper primary meal carry different figures.

Why it looks reasonable: the working counted two lines and two unknowns and drew the usual conclusion, and counting lines is what most people do. The substitution was carried out correctly. And 25 with 25 is a pair that does satisfy the statement, so checking it back against the note would not have caught this either. The only thing that catches it is asking whether the second line says anything new.

blocks.prompt:
A programme note says this about a school kitchen.

Between last year and this year the kitchen’s total number of meals went up, and its total kilocalories went up. So it served more lower primary meals and more upper primary meals than it did last year.

Schedule II of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets the lower primary hot cooked meal at 450 kilocalories. It sets the upper primary hot cooked meal at 700 kilocalories. Take last year as 30 lower primary meals and 20 upper primary meals a day. Those two counts are made up for this problem.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: whether a pair of counts exists in which both totals rise and one of the two counts falls. If one does, the claim does not follow, whatever this kitchen actually did.

Start with last year’s two totals.

30 plus 20 = 50

450 times 30 = 13,500
700 times 20 = 14,000
13,500 plus 14,000 = 27,500

Fifty meals and 27,500 kilocalories.

Now try this year as 26 lower primary meals and 25 upper primary meals.

26 plus 25 = 51

450 times 26 = 11,700
700 times 25 = 17,500
11,700 plus 17,500 = 29,200

Fifty-one meals and 29,200 kilocalories. Both totals went up. The lower primary count went down, from 30 to 26.

So the claim does not follow. Two totals are two statements about two unknowns, and knowing that both totals rose is not knowing either unknown. The upper primary meal carries a larger figure, so shifting meals towards it lifts the kilocalorie total even while one count falls.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that the lower primary count actually fell, and nothing here says the note’s conclusion is false. It says the two totals do not reach it. It also does not establish what the kitchen did at all, because the counts used here were invented to test the reasoning. And it says nothing about whether any child ate a meal, since a meal counted and a meal eaten are two different things.

What to ask for instead: both counts for both years. Two counts and two totals for one year would also do it, because then you have two statements and two unknowns and the pair solves.
